market_context: United States; lactose and dairy foods
title: Which Foods Have Lactose, and Which Contain Very Little?

seo.title: Foods With Lactose and Foods With Very Little
seo.meta_description: Milk, ice cream, and fresh dairy provide more lactose; aged cheese and butter usually contain little. Tolerance depends on the total dose, not simply whether a food is dairy.
seo.search_intent: Identify foods with high, moderate, and low amounts of lactose.

excerpt: Milk and many fresh dairy foods provide several grams of lactose per serving; yogurt often contains less or is better tolerated because of fermentation. Aged cheeses and butter contain much smaller amounts because lactose leaves with whey or is fermented.
content_html:
“Dairy” does not mean “high lactose.” The amount changes dramatically depending on how much watery milk phase remains and whether bacteria have fermented the sugar.

Milk is the useful reference point

One cup of milk contains roughly 12 grams of lactose. Ice cream, milkshakes, and dairy desserts can also provide meaningful amounts, depending on the recipe and serving.

Fermentation changes tolerance

Yogurt still contains lactose, but live cultures produce lactase, and many people with lactose maldigestion tolerate yogurt better than the same amount of milk.

Aged cheeses contain very little

During cheesemaking, much of the lactose leaves in whey and the remainder continues to ferment during aging. Parmesan, aged cheddar, and similar cheeses can contain only trace amounts per serving. Butter is also low because it is mostly milk fat.

Intolerance is not milk allergy

Lactose intolerance depends on dose and digestion. Milk-protein allergy is an immune reaction, and a lactose-free dairy product still contains milk proteins. For lactose intolerance, the actual grams in a serving matter more than a simple dairy yes-or-no list.

faq.question: Does cheese contain lactose?
faq.answer: Fresh cheeses can contain more, while long-aged cheeses usually contain very little.

faq.question: Does butter contain lactose?
faq.answer: Yes, but typically only a small amount per serving because butter is mostly fat.

faq.question: Is lactose-free milk safe for a milk allergy?
faq.answer: No. Removing or splitting lactose does not remove the milk proteins that trigger allergy.
